title: How to evaluate AI takeoff software on a job you already know the answer to
summary: Evaluate AI takeoff software on a job you already priced by hand, not on the vendor’s demo file. Here’s the test, and the places it usually breaks.
body_markdown:
The vendor’s demo file always works. It was chosen because it works. The question that actually matters is what happens when you hand the thing your worst set from last quarter.


Every estimator in a trial asks the same question, and it’s the right one. How accurate is it. The problem is that the question has no answer in the abstract, and the demo is structured to prevent you from finding one. A salesperson runs a clean set, the counts come back, and you’ve learned nothing you can use. The way to evaluate


[AI takeoff](https://fresco.build/ai-takeoff-software) software is to stop watching someone else’s job and run your own, on a package where you already know what the answer should be.


## The demo file was chosen because it works


A demo proves the software runs. It doesn’t tell you how it behaves on your work.


This isn’t a complaint about vendors. Any reasonable person demonstrating a product picks a file that shows it well, and the files that show these tools well are the ones with a clean schedule, a consistent drawing set, and no addenda. That describes very few of the jobs actually sitting on your desk.


The gap matters more here than in most software categories, because a door and hardware takeoff isn’t a counting problem. It’s a reconciliation problem. The schedule says one thing, the floor plan says another, the elevation says a third, and the 087100 specification says something that contradicts all of them. Software that counts doors well on a clean set hasn’t been asked the question your job will ask it.


One distributor owner put his evaluation goal plainly. He wasn’t trying to confirm it worked. He said he was “curious to locate any bugs that there could be or anywhere where it’s like underdeveloped.”


That’s the correct posture, and it needs a job to point at.


## Start with a package you’ve already priced by hand


The single most useful thing you can bring to a trial is a job you finished, and the time it took you.


An estimator at a general contractor described doing exactly this. He had kept a running log of his own hours on a 280 opening job, by hand, start to finish, and he wanted to “take that same job and recreate that.” Someone else on the same call put it a different way, that the point was to “compare it to like our manual process to see like how how accurate was it really?”


That comparison is the only one that means anything, because it’s the only one where you already hold the answer key. You know how many openings there were. You know which ones were wrong on the drawings. You know what you qualified and what you ate. When the software returns a number, you aren’t evaluating a claim. You’re checking a result.


Two practical notes on choosing the job. It should be recent enough that you remember the arguments, and it should be a real bid rather than a job you built as an exercise. Reconstructed jobs are always cleaner than the thing that actually happened.


If you never logged your hours, log them on the next one before you start a trial. A week of note taking buys you a baseline that no vendor can give you.


## The set that gave you trouble is the only set worth running


Test on your worst package, not your best one.


The instinct is to pick something representative. Resist it. A representative job tells you the software works on jobs where everything works, which you could have guessed. The package worth running is the one where the architect’s schedule disagreed with the plans, or the hardware sets arrived in an addendum, or half the openings were missing their handing.


A Division 8 specialist evaluating a tool had a specific case in mind from his own work: “The patio doors were not marked at any of the plans. I just wondered if it flagged them.” That’s a good test, because he already knew the answer and the software didn’t.


A solo estimator running his own trial said something similar about his local architect. “The architect has exactly those two problems for us.” He wasn’t curious whether the software could count doors. He wanted to know whether it would catch the two specific things that firm gets wrong on every job it designs, which is a narrower question and a much more useful one.


Bring the job that made you angry. You’ll learn more in twenty minutes than a month of clean sets will teach you.


## What the software does with missing information is the whole test


The most important behavior to check isn’t accuracy. It’s what happens when the drawings don’t say.


A door schedule that omits handing, a frame with no wall thickness given, an opening that appears on the plan and not in the schedule: these aren’t edge cases, they’re most of a Division 8 package. There are only two things a piece of software can do when it hits one, and the difference between them is the difference between a tool and a liability.


It can flag the gap and ask you. Or it can fill the gap with its best guess and keep going. Which fields a given tool even attempts is worth establishing early, and we’ve covered


[what these tools actually read in a Division 8 set](https://fresco.build/blog/ai-door-takeoff-what-it-reads-division-8-set) in detail.


A guess that’s right is indistinguishable from a guess that’s wrong until the doors show up. So the behavior you want is the one that refuses: software that errors out rather than assuming, and that tells you which opening it couldn’t resolve and why. Sorting flags is work, and it’s visible work you can price. A silent assumption is invisible work that surfaces as a change order.


Design the test around this directly. Take your package, find three openings where you know the drawings are incomplete, and see what comes back. A list of flags is a pass. A complete schedule with no flags on an incomplete set isn’t an impressive result. It’s a warning.


## Wall type is the field that fails most often on a first run


Check every wall type assignment by hand on your first test job, because this is the field that fails most often and announces itself least.


Wall type drives frame depth, frame depth drives the frame, and the frame isn’t a cheap thing to get wrong. The information is also genuinely hard to extract: it lives in a partition schedule on a different sheet, it’s often keyed by a symbol rather than written out, and the total assembly thickness is frequently not stated anywhere at all, because the architect expects you to add up the layers.


In live evaluations this is a recurring sticking point. Teams have found the drywall layers correctly identified while the total thickness was never given on the drawings in the first place, which is a drawing problem rather than a software problem but lands on the estimator either way. Others have found wall type assignment to be the area needing the most human correction.


Two things follow. First, don’t accept a wall type column at face value on any tool. Second, when you find errors here, trace them back before you blame the software. A meaningful share of them turn out to be errors in the source documents, which the software has faithfully reproduced. That distinction matters for your evaluation, and it also tells you something useful about the architect.


## Check what it did to your manufacturers, not just your counts


Run a column by column comparison of specified manufacturers between the source documents and the output.


Counts are easy to check and everybody checks them. Manufacturer and product line substitutions are easy to miss and expensive to miss, because a hardware set that reads correctly at a glance can carry a different lockset than the one you specified. Evaluation teams have found exactly this: output where the specified manufacturer had been changed, with nothing in the result announcing the change.


Sometimes the substitution is the feature working as intended. Value engineering tools exist to propose equivalents, and a proposed equivalent clearly marked as a proposal is useful. The thing to establish during a trial is whether your tool distinguishes between the two, and whether the distinction survives the export.


The test is mechanical. Pick one hardware set from your own job, read the specification, and compare every line. Then do a second set. If the two agree with your source, you can start trusting the column.


## Stacked and duplicated openings are a known failure mode, so test for them


Count your doors twice, once in the software and once on the plan, on any job with repeated units.


Duplicate counting has a specific cause in this trade. On multifamily and hospitality plans, identical units stack vertically, and drawings frequently show the same opening in more than one place: once on a unit plan, once on an enlarged plan, once in a typical detail. Software reading all of them can legitimately see three doors where there’s one. Teams running multifamily packages in evaluation have hit exactly this, and have also hit imports that came through missing opening numbers entirely, which is the same problem from the other direction.


If you run multifamily work, this is your first test, not an afterthought. Take a building with twelve identical units, run it, and check the total against the unit count times the doors per unit. The arithmetic is trivial and it will tell you in two minutes what a week of general use might not.


We’ve written separately on


[why the same opening gets counted twice on a large plan](https://fresco.build/blog/match-line-double-counting-door-takeoffs) .


## The export is part of the product, and it fails later than the takeoff does


Test the export into your actual system during the trial, not after you buy.


This is the step most evaluations skip, and it’s the one that most often turns a successful trial into a stalled rollout. The takeoff can be correct and still arrive in your estimating or order entry system with the fields in the wrong places. In live evaluations, field mapping into existing systems has repeatedly been the bottleneck rather than the extraction itself, and the problem doesn’t surface until somebody tries to use the output for real.


So run the whole path. Export a finished job, import it into Comsense or eMullion or whatever you actually run, and look at what landed. Check that opening numbers carried, that hardware sets stayed attached to their openings, and that your pricing structure survived. If the vendor offers custom field mapping, that’s a good sign, but have them do it on your file during the trial rather than promising it afterward.


Unusual document formatting is worth a second pass here too. Hardware extraction that works on a conventionally laid out schedule can fail on a schedule built in an unusual template, and distributors see plenty of those.


## A confidence score is a claim you’re supposed to check


Where the software reports confidence, spend your first session finding out what the numbers actually mean.


Several tools in this category now attach confidence scores to inferred fields, typically door swing, wall thickness and handing. This is a genuinely good design. It’s also easy to misread as a quality guarantee, when what it really is is a list sorted by where to look first.


The useful test is calibration. Take the twenty openings with the lowest reported confidence and check them all by hand. Then take twenty of the highest and check those. What you want to find is that the low scores are where the errors cluster. If errors are evenly distributed across confidence levels, the score isn’t telling you anything and you’ll need to check everything regardless, which changes your estimate of what the tool saves you.


Ask one more question while you’re there: how does revision work. If an addendum lands and you re-run the job, does that cost you a full charge? Some credit models re-run revisions at no cost, which materially changes how a job behaves over a bid cycle, and you won’t discover it by reading the pricing page.


## The same test works on something you built yourself


If your plan is to build this in-house, run the identical protocol against your own build.


This has become a real option. A capable person with a current AI coding assistant can assemble something that reads a door schedule and produces a table, and some estimating teams have concluded that what they built is good enough. That might be true. The point is that “good enough” is a measurement, and almost nobody who says it has made one.


Run your own tool against the job you already priced by hand. Check the wall types, check the manufacturers, check the duplicate openings, check what it does with the three openings you know are incomplete, and check the export. The protocol doesn’t care who wrote the software.


What usually surfaces isn’t that the in-house build is bad. It’s that it handles the common case well and has no behavior at all for the uncommon one, and Division 8 is a trade where the uncommon case is where the money is. That’s worth knowing before it’s load bearing on a bid.


There’s a reason the bar is set where it is. We’ve written before about


[why estimators distrust what these tools return](https://fresco.build/blog/why-estimators-dont-trust-ai-takeoffs) , and a commenter on the estimating subreddit framed it bluntly: “this system would have to be insanely good for me to consider trusting it with takeoffs.” That standard should apply to the thing you built as well.


## What to run before you decide


**Price one job by hand and keep the clock.** Without a logged baseline you have no comparison, and a vendor’s time saving claim is a number about somebody else’s job. If you have no logged job, log the next one before the trial starts.


**Run your worst package, not a representative one.** Pick the job where the schedule and the plans disagreed. Clean sets tell you the software works on clean sets.


**Check three known gaps on purpose.** Find three openings where the drawings genuinely don’t say, and confirm the software flags them rather than filling them in. Flags are the product working.


**Audit wall types and manufacturers line by line on the first job.** These two fields fail most often and are the easiest to accept at a glance. Trace any errors back to the source documents before concluding the tool was wrong.


**Export into your real system before you sign anything.** Run the full path into Comsense, eMullion or whatever you use, and confirm opening numbers and hardware set associations survived. Field mapping is where good trials stall.


## When this doesn’t apply


If your work is overhead or garage doors, or you’re a labor only installer with no hardware scope, none of this is aimed at you. These tools read Division 8 pedestrian openings, and a protocol for testing them isn’t useful if that’s not what you price.


If you bid two or three small jobs a month off drawings you already know well, the honest answer is that a careful manual takeoff is competitive and the evaluation may not be worth your week. The argument for this software gets stronger as opening counts and package complexity rise, and it’s weak at the bottom end.


And if what you actually need is order entry, submittal tracking and job management after award, that’s a different category of product. Several of these tools cover the pre-bid work well and stop at the win. Know which problem you’re shopping for before you start testing, because a trial that evaluates the wrong half will give you a clean answer to a question you didn’t have.


## Key takeaways


- The only meaningful accuracy test is a job you’ve already priced by hand, because it’s the only one where you hold the answer key before the software runs.
- Software that flags missing information is behaving correctly, and a complete schedule returned from an incomplete drawing set is a warning rather than a result.
- Wall type assignment and manufacturer substitution are the two fields that fail most often in live evaluations, and both are easy to accept at a glance.
- Export field mapping into an existing system is where more trials stall than extraction ever does, which is why it belongs inside the trial rather than after it.
- A buyer evaluating something they built in-house needs the same protocol, because “good enough” is a measurement and most people who say it haven’t made one.


## Frequently asked questions


### How long should a trial of AI takeoff software actually take?


Long enough to run one complete job from drawings through export, which is usually a few days rather than a few weeks. Running many jobs shallowly teaches you less than running one job all the way through. If you can’t complete a full path in the trial window, ask for more time rather than deciding on a partial result.


### What accuracy rate should I expect from AI takeoff software?


Ask instead what the software does when it’s unsure, because that’s the number that affects your bid. A tool that resolves 85 percent of openings and clearly flags the rest is more useful than one claiming 95 percent with no indication of which openings are the uncertain ones. Accuracy without visibility isn’t usable.


### Does AI takeoff software replace the estimator?


No, and a tool that claims to is making a claim you can test in an afternoon. Code interpretation, bid strategy, qualification language and the decision about what to do with a flagged opening all stay with the estimator. What changes is how long it takes to get to the point where those decisions are the only work left.


### Can I test it on a job I’m currently bidding?


You can, but it’s a worse test than a completed job, because you have no verified answer to check against and the bid deadline will push you toward accepting output you haven’t audited. Use a finished job for evaluation. Use a live job once you’ve already established where the tool is weak.


### What if the software gets a wall type wrong?


Trace it back to the drawings before you record it as a software error. A meaningful share of wall type errors in live evaluations turn out to be faithful reproductions of a problem in the source documents, where the partition schedule is keyed by symbol or the total assembly thickness is never stated. Both outcomes are worth knowing, and they’re different findings.


Run it on a job you already finished. Fresco’s
